summary.summary: Telford & Wrekin's debt is stepping up: external borrowing rose £57.8m in the year to £492.7m and the borrowing need rose £63.5m to £668.4m, against an authorised ceiling of £665m for debt. Capital spending came in at £113.3m against an original £151.6m plan. Short-term investments stood at £23.9m.

signals.headline: External debt up £57.8m to £492.7m; CFR up £63.5m to £668.4m
signals.why: A material step-up in real borrowing with headroom to the authorised limit narrowing.

compliance.notes: Strong on treasury mechanics: liability benchmark charted to 2077/78, creditworthiness policy using CDS/watches beyond ratings, borrowing strategy that explains the under-borrowed position, an MRP statement with asset-life justification and VRP disclosure, comprehensive counterparty/country limits, and an ESG/ethical framework integrated into lending. Weakest on non-treasury/commercial disclosure: the TMSS explicitly defers all service/commercial investment content (proportionality to financial capacity, statutory security/fair-value and income-dependence-with-contingency disclosures, exit review, and service/commercial limits) to a separate Investment Strategy & Capital Strategy report (Cabinet 12 Feb / Full Council 26 Feb 2026) not in this bundle, so COM-07/08/09 are absent and COM-03 (core) is only partial despite ~£235m of NuPlace/PIP CFR exposure. Also incomplete: the financing-costs-to-net-revenue-stream ratio (current year only), no audit-qualification flag, and half-yearly rather than explicitly quarterly indicator monitoring. Scored from the 28 Jan 2026 Audit Committee report bundle (recommended to Full Council 26 Feb 2026).

news_drafts.headline: Telford and Wrekin's SEND plan approved, unlocking £8.3m grant against £9.21m schools deficit
news_drafts.lead:
The Department for Education approved Telford and Wrekin Council's local plan for reforming support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) on 2 October 2026. That makes the council eligible for the High Needs Stability Grant of about £8.3m, which it expects to receive at the end of November 2026, according to the 2026/27 financial monitoring report going to Cabinet.

The grant is aimed at the council's dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit, an overspend on the government grant that funds schools, in this case mainly on support for children with special needs. The council carried forward a deficit of £9.21m from 2025/26. The £8.3m covers 90% of that. The council holds £430k in reserves, money it has put aside, to fund the remaining 10% by 31 March 2028.

The report also sets out the pressure in the current year. The council expects the in-year deficit on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, to be "in the region of £10m" in 2026/27. The paper puts this down to "increasing numbers of children and young people needing additional educational support" across the high needs system, and says the reform plans will take time to have a significant effect on growing demand. The papers also record a £0.9m transfer from the schools block to high needs.

findings.headline: Net borrowing at £524.9m is £26m below the original estimate, but Capital Financing Requirement forecast to rise to £648.8m by 2028/29.
findings.detail: The council's actual net borrowing at end-August 2026 was £524.9m, favourable to the original estimate of £550.7m. However, the Capital Financing Requirement (the amount permitted to borrow for capital) is forecast to rise significantly: £597.3m in 2027/28 and £648.8m in 2028/29. Treasury management indicators remain within policy limits, with financing costs at 7.64% of revenue. The council holds no investments beyond one year and maintains a good credit score (1.74 out of target 6 or lower).
findings.matters: Rising CFR indicates the council is planning material increases in capital borrowing over the next two years; this affects debt headroom and future debt servicing costs, and may require accelerated capital delivery or extended payback periods.
findings.figures: Net borrowing Aug 2026: £524.9m vs estimate £550.7m; CFR forecast 2027/28: £597.3m; 2028/29: £648.8m; Financing cost ratio: 7.64% of revenue
findings.quote: Overall Treasury Portfolio at 31 August 2026 - £m... Net Borrowing 550.7 524.9 597.3 648.8... Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) (Loans)... CFR (above) is below both the Authorised Limit and the Operational Boundary

findings.headline: Council forecasting net revenue overspend of £3.95m, held by £1.53m council-wide underspend rather than service savings.
findings.detail: The council's total forecast is a £3.95m revenue overspend. This is being offset by a £1.53m council-wide underspend (from lower-than-budgeted inflation and contingency costs) and underspends in Finance, Policy & Governance, Housing and Neighbourhood services. The overspend is therefore dependent on these offsetting items holding; it is not being resolved through savings programmes but through unused contingencies.
findings.matters: Managing an overspend through contingency drawdown rather than active mitigation is a sustainability risk; contingencies deplete, leaving future years without flexibility if service pressures persist.
findings.figures: Total forecasted overspend: £3,949,726; Council Wide mitigation: (£1,529,572); Children's overspend: £3,104,804; Adult Care: £696,150; Education: £925,835; Prosperity: £963,777

findings.headline: Education service overspend of £926k includes £296k growth in premature retirement pension costs (closed scheme), with a further £300k growth committed from 2027/28.
findings.detail: Education & Skills is forecasting a £926k overspend. Of this, £296k is growth in costs for a closed premature retirement pension scheme that the council remains obliged to fund. The council is building in a further £300k annual growth from 2027/28, indicating this is a structural cost that will continue to escalate. Other pressures include school transport (£97k) and specialist services for statutory assessments (£234k).
findings.matters: Closed pension liabilities that continue to inflate are a fixed, unavoidable cost; the escalation built into forward years indicates the council accepts this is a permanent budget pressure without solution.
findings.figures: £925,835 service overspend; £295,701 premature retirement cost increase; £300k committed growth from 27/28; £233,918 specialist services overspend
findings.quote: This policy ceased some years ago however, the local authority remains responsible for any historic pension costs and additional costs are due to inflationary pressures. £300k growth built into corporate model from 27/28

findings.headline: Wellington Market refurbishment requiring £268k annual trader support with reduced rental income while work continues.
findings.detail: Wellington Market is incurring £268k support costs for traders during its refurbishment, with rental income significantly reduced as a result. This represents an ongoing commitment beyond the capital investment in the market upgrade and extends the total cost of the regeneration scheme.
findings.matters: Extended or larger-than-planned support costs for town centre regeneration indicate scheme complexity or slower-than-expected trader recovery; this extends the revenue impact of what was presented as a capital investment.
findings.figures: £267,529 trader support cost; reduced rental income
findings.quote: Ongoing support to traders throughout the refurbishment of  Wellington Market resulting in a reduced rental income

findings.headline: Property Investment Portfolio income shortfall of £735k attributed to void properties, plus £228k cost overspend on landlord responsibilities.
findings.detail: The Prosperity & Investment service is forecasting a £964k overspend. Of this, £735k is income shortfall on the Property Investment Portfolio driven by vacant units, and £228k is cost overspend relating to landlord liabilities (maintenance, utilities, rates on empty properties). A separate shortfall of £229k is forecast on BiT income projections. Premises cost underspends partially offset these pressures.
findings.matters: Void costs on investment property are a drag on net return; prolonged voids signal either property quality issues, market weakness, or portfolio mismanagement.
findings.figures: £963,777 service overspend; £735,212 PIP income shortfall; £228,378 PIP property cost overspend; £228,632 BiT income shortfall
findings.quote: Shortfall in income reflects the projected impact of  a number of void properties
